newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australian Broadcasting Corp Morning Update.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australian Broadcasting Corp Morning Update.

text.p: MEMORIAL SERVICE TO BE HELD FOR VICTIMS OF SLIDE
In Western Australia, up to five-thousand people are expected to attend a memorial service this morning for the victims of the Cowaramup rock slide.
Nine local people died almost a week ago in the cliff collapse at Gracetown.
The local member for Vasse and former Cowaramup Bay primary school student, Barry Blaikie, has made a plea to the media to honour a code of sensitivity in their coverage of the memorial service.
Television and newspaper crews have been asked to keep their distance from up to 300 surfers who'll paddle off the coast of Gracetown as a final tribute.
GOVT SEEKS ADIVCE ON HUMAN RIGHTS DECISION
The Queensland Government says it's seeking legal advice on a decision by the Human Rights and Equal Opportunity Commission to award six Aborigines compensation, before making a response.
The Commission has found that discriminatory work practices on Palm Island off Townsville, between 1975 and 1984, had resulted in the Aborigines being paid less than white workers.
They're to be paid seven-thousand dollars in compensation and will also receive a public apology.
The government has three options -- appeal the decision, don't comply and probably end up in the Federal and High Courts, or pay.
STONE SAYS NORTHERN TERRITORY SHOULD BE A STATE
The Chief Minister last night told 3-hundred CLP supporters in Darwin why the Territory should become a state.
Shane Stone says the Territory's had seventeen years of self Government, and is about to turn 21 and it's time to "leave home".
Mr Stone says he wants to inform as many Territorians as possible about constitutional development and the push to become a state by the year 2001.
LAWYER SAYS ABORIGINAL VICTORY STILL SIGNIFICANT
In North Queensland, Aboriginal elders on Palm Island off
Townsville, say a compensation award made to Aborigines who
suffered discrimination is insulting and inadequate.
The Human Rights and Equal Opportunity Commission has ordered the Queensland Government to pay six Aborigines seven-thousand dollars each and publicly apologise to them.
Ten years ago, seven Palm Island residents alleged that between 1975 and 1984, they were discriminated against by the Queensland Government.
They say they were paid wages at a rate less than non-Aboriginal workers.
Jean Sibley, who missed out on receiving compensation, says no one is happy with the compensation.
But their lawyer, Bob Haebich, says it's still a significant victory.
STUDY FINDS WOMEN GETTING MORE OBESE
A new study has found that Australian women are getting at a huge cost to the health system.
The University of Newcastle study on women's health looked at over 14-thousand women nationally.
It found there was a four per cent increase in the proportion of obese middle aged women, compared to figures from a national health foundation survey in 1989.
Doctor Wendy Brown, who delivered a paper to a Public Health Association conference in Perth yesterday, says there's a corresponding increase in health problems, such as diabetes and hypertension.
As a result, Doctor Brown says women are utilising health services more.
YANNER SAYS HAYDEN CAN'T HEAR

An Aboriginal Leader says someone better than former Governor General Bill Hayden, could have sent to head negotiations over the future of the proposed billion-dollar zinc mine in far north-west Queensland.
Co-ordinator of the Carpentaria Land Council, Murandoo Yanner, says
Mr Hayden is not up to the task, beacuse a hearing disability is preventing him from being an effective negotiator.
Speaking in Townsville, Mr Yanner also says Bill Hayden has never had any association with, or sympathy for Aboriginal people at any time in his life or his political career.
IR TALKS THE LONGEST BUT STILL NO AGREEMENT
The Federal Government says it's still hopefull its industrial relations reforms will be up and running in the New Year.
Industrial Relations Minister Peter Reith and the Australian Democrats met late into last night, in an attempt to reach agreement on the Workplace Relations Bill.
The seven-hour meeting was the fourteenth and longest meeting in six months of negotiations.
The main sticking points appear to be the award system and the role of the Industrial Relations Commission and Employment Advocate in ratifying individual contracts.
None of the parties are commenting on negotiation details or how close to agreement they are.
GREEN PUSH TO BAN NUCLEAR SHIPS FROM TASMANIA
The Tasmanian Greens have given a message direct to the U.S. consul that visits by nuclear warships are not welcome in the state.
Green M.P. Mike Foley has confirmed he handed the consul a motion pointing out that most members of the House of Assembly oppose visits by nuclear powered or armed ships.
The moves comes on the eve of a parliamentary debate on Green legislation to prohibit servicing of warships in Tasmanian ports.
However, the Labor leader, Michael Field says although his party also opposes nuclear warship visits, it won't support the Greens' legislation.
Labor has introduced a counter motion calling on the State
Government to lobby the Commonwealth to declare Tasmanian waters nuclear free.
CAMPBELL TAKES FIRST STEP IN PARTY
The Federal member for Kalgoorlie, Graeme Campbell has taken the first formal step in establishing his own political party.
Mr Campbell's Australia First Party has been registered both Federally and in Western Australia.
Registration in the other states is proceeding.
Mr Campbell says the party has five main objectives:

To stop the multi-cultural push to make Australia a part of Asia; establish manufacturing industry; introduce citizen's initiated referenda; stop the growing rift between rural and urban Australia and help small business.
SCIENCE CONFERENCE CONCLUDES
Members of the international science community today wind up a conference in Canberra with presentations on economic threats to global security and the need for industrial research.
The 65th ANZAAS Congress has covered topics including water pollution, toxic waste, land degredation, and the loss of biodiversity.
Presentations have also been made on challenges likely in the 21st
century, such as the spread of infectious diseases.
The conference has heard the emerging science of biotechnology is being used in developing vaccines to help increase animal productivity.
BUILDING WORK THREATENED DURING OLYMPICS
The Construction Union says it's members are not prepared to be displaced from work in the City of Sydney during the year 2000 Olympics Draft legislation would allow the Planning Minister to stop
building work during the Games.
But Construction Union Secretary Andrew Ferguson says building workers on casual day hire would be seriously hurt if their projects were stalled for six weeks during the Olympics.

He says the union has written to the Labor Council seeking urgent talks with the State Government. A spokesman for Local Government Minister Ernie Page says the bill is out for consultation, and all views will be taken into account.
-- Reuters Sydney Newsroom 61-2 373-1800
